title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 818–819 (Night 175, continuing nights-174), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 175 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān accepts the vizier's counsel of fifteen days' imprisonment, but he cannot rest: every night he had slept only with his arm beneath his son's neck, and now he tosses as though on embers of ghaḍā, and weeping recites two poems on a night that will not end. In the tower, the servant brings Qamar al-Zamān a lantern, lights a candle in a candlestick and sets food before him; the prince eats a little, reproaches himself for his disrespect to his father, telling his soul that a son of Adam is hostage to his tongue, weeps and recites verses on the slip of the tongue that costs a man his head. Then the mamluk washes his hands, and he makes his ablutions, prays the sunset and night prayers and sits down, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-fifth night,
sentences.n: The formula as before, with al-khāmisa, “the fifth”, feminine to agree with layla: the units first, joined to the tens by wa-, and baʿda al-miʾati, “after the hundred”, for the hundreds.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ قَالَ لِلْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ دَعْ وَلَدَكَ فِى السِّجْنِ مُدَّةَ خَمْسَةَ عَشَرَ يَوْمًا ثُمَّ أَحْضِرْهُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْكَ وَأْمُرْهُ بِالزَّوَاجِ فَإِنَّهُ لَا يُخَالِفُكَ أَبَدًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-wazīra qāla li-al-maliki Shahramāna daʿ waladaka fī al-sijni muddata khamsata ʿashara yawman thumma aḥḍirhu bayna yadayka wa-ʾmurhu bi-al-zawāji fa-innahu lā yukhālifuka abadan
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-vizier said to-the-king Shahramān: Leave your-son in the-prison (a) period of five-ten day, then bring-him between your-two-hands and command-him with-the-marriage; for indeed-he will-not oppose-you ever.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier said to King Shahramān, “Leave your son in prison for fifteen days, then bring him before you and command him to marry. He will never go against you.”
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the vizier's advice from the end of the last night, word for word. li-al-maliki, “to the king”: li- marks the one spoken to, and the alif of the article is not written after it (لل). khamsata ʿashara yawman, “fifteen days”, the number with its noun in the accusative singular. In wa-ʾmurhu the print writes the hamza itself (وأمره). amara chooses bi- for what is commanded: bi-al-zawāji, “to marry”. The print writes في as فى, as it often does.

sentences.t: فَقَبِلَ الْمَلِكُ رَأْيَ الْوَزِيرِ فِي ذَلِكَ وَنَامَ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ وَهُوَ مُشْتَغِلُ الْقَلْبِ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ يُحِبُّهُ مَحَبَّةً عَظِيمَةً حَيْثُ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ وَلَدٌ سِوَاهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qabila al-maliku raʾya al-wazīri fī dhālika wa-nāma tilka al-laylata wa-huwa mushtaghilu al-qalbi ʿalā waladihi li-annahu kāna yuḥibbuhu maḥabbatan ʿaẓīmatan ḥaythu lam yakun lahu waladun siwāhu
sentences.l: So accepted the-king (the) opinion of the-vizier in that, and slept that the-night, and he (was) busy of the-heart over his-son, because he used-to love-him a-love great, since not was to-him a-son other-than-him.
sentences.i: The king accepted the vizier's counsel in this, and went to sleep that night with his heart full of care for his son; for he loved him dearly, having no son but him.
sentences.n: The print has والده, “his father”, a misprint for ولده, “his son”, corrected here: the king's care is for Qamar al-Zamān, as the rest of the sentence shows. mushtaghilu al-qalbi ʿalā, “busy of heart over”, is “anxious about”: the adjective stands in construct with the noun it qualifies, like munkasiru al-khāṭiri in the last night, and ʿalā marks the one worried over. li-annahu, “because he”: li-, “for (the reason)”, with anna. yuḥibbuhu maḥabbatan ʿaẓīmatan, “loved him a great love”: a noun of the verb's own meaning in the accusative (the absolute object) to say how much. ḥaythu, “since, seeing that”, as often in this text. The hamza of رأي and the shadda of يحبّه are printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ كُلَّ لَيْلَةٍ لَمْ يَجِىءْ لَهُ نَوْمٌ إِلَّا إِذَا وَضَعَ ذِرَاعَهُ تَحْتَ رَقَبَةِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَيَنَامُ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna al-maliku Shahramānu kulla laylatin lam yajīʾ lahu nawmun illā idhā waḍaʿa dhirāʿahu taḥta raqabati Qamari al-Zamāni wa-yanāmu
sentences.l: And was the-king Shahramān, every night, not came to-him sleep except when he-put his-arm under (the) neck of Qamar al-Zamān, and-he-sleeps.
sentences.i: Every night, King Shahramān could find no sleep unless he laid his arm beneath Qamar al-Zamān's neck, and so he would sleep.
sentences.n: Father and son, we learn, slept side by side. kāna … lam yajīʾ lahu nawmun, “was … sleep did not come to him”: kāna sets the clause after it in the past, as a habit. kulla laylatin, accusative of time, “every night”. After lam Classical Arabic shortens the vowel, lam yajiʾ (لم يجئ); the print keeps the long ī (يجىء), a common Middle Arabic habit, and it is read so here. illā idhā, “except when”. wa-yanāmu, “and he sleeps”, an imperfect run on loosely after the perfect waḍaʿa: “and then he would sleep”.

sentences.t: فَبَاتَ الْمَلِكُ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ مُتَشَوِّشَ الْخَاطِرِ مِنْ أَجْلِهِ وَصَارَ يَتَقَلَّبُ مِنْ جَنْبٍ إِلَى جَنْبٍ كَأَنَّهُ نَائِمٌ عَلَى جَمْرِ الْغَضَاةِ
sentences.tr: fa-bāta al-maliku tilka al-laylata mutashawwisha al-khāṭiri min ajlihi wa-ṣāra yataqallabu min janbin ilā janbin ka-annahu nāʾimun ʿalā jamri al-ghaḍāti
sentences.l: So passed-the-night the-king that the-night troubled of the-mind for his-sake, and began tossing from side to side, as-though-he (were) sleeping on (the) embers of the-ghaḍā.
sentences.i: So the king spent that night troubled in mind on his son's account, tossing from side to side as though he lay on embers of ghaḍā wood.
sentences.n: bāta, “to pass the night”, takes mutashawwisha al-khāṭiri, “troubled of mind”, as its predicate, in the accusative. mutashawwish, “confused, disturbed”, Form V from shawwasha, is a post-Classical word. ṣāra with the imperfect, “began to, went on”. jamr al-ghaḍā, “embers of ghaḍā”, is a stock image of torment: ghaḍā is a desert shrub whose wood burns long and fiercely. The print spells it الغضاة, with a tāʾ marbūṭa, a Middle Arabic spelling of al-ghaḍā; it is kept and read al-ghaḍāti. The ئ of نائم and the shadda of كانّه are printed.

sentences.t: وَلَحِقَهُ الْوَسْوَاسُ وَلَمْ يَأْخُذْهُ نَوْمٌ فِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةِ بِطُولِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-laḥiqahu al-waswāsu wa-lam yaʾkhudhhu nawmun fī tilka al-laylati bi-ṭūlihā
sentences.l: And overtook-him the-whispering, and not took-him sleep in that the-night with-its-length.
sentences.i: Brooding fears came upon him, and no sleep took him all that night long.
sentences.n: waswās, “whispering”, is the inner whisper of anxious, nagging thoughts. akhadhahu al-nawmu, “sleep took him”, is the ordinary idiom for falling asleep; here lam with the jussive yaʾkhudhhu. bi-ṭūlihā, “with its length”: bi- here “throughout”, the whole length of the night.

sentences.t: وَذَرَفَتْ عَيْنَاهُ بِالدُّمُوعِ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: wa-dharafat ʿaynāhu bi-al-dumūʿi wa-anshada yaqūlu shiʿrun
sentences.l: And shed his-two-eyes with-the-tears, and he-recited, saying — verse:
sentences.i: His eyes overflowed with tears, and he recited these lines:
sentences.n: dharafat ʿaynāhu bi-al-dumūʿi, “his eyes streamed with tears”: bi- marks what they pour out. ʿaynāhu is the dual, “his two eyes”, with a feminine verb because ʿayn is feminine. شعر, “verse”, is the print's rubric announcing the poem.

sentences.t:
لَقَدْ طَالَ لَيْلِي وَالْوُشَاةُ هُجُوْعُ * وَنَاهِيْكَ قَلْبًا بِالْفِرَاقِ مَرُوْعُ
اُقُوْلُ وَلَيْلِيْ زَادَ بِالْهَمِّ طُوْلَهُ * اَمَا لَكَ يَا ضُوْءَ الصَّبَاحِ رُجُوْعُ
sentences.tr:
laqad ṭāla laylī wa-al-wushātu hujūʿu * wa-nāhīka qalban bi-al-firāqi marūʿu
uqūlu wa-laylī zāda bi-al-hammi ṭūlahu * amā laka yā ḍūʾa al-ṣabāḥi rujūʿu
sentences.l:
Indeed has-grown-long my-night, while the-talebearers (are) sleepers; * and enough-for-you (as) a-heart, by-the-parting terrified!
I-say, while my-night has-increased with-the-care its-length: * Is there not for-you, O light of the-morning, (a) return?
sentences.i:
Long has my night become, while the talebearers sleep; and what a heart is mine, struck with terror by parting!
I say, as my night grows longer with sorrow, “O light of morning, will you never return?”
sentences.n: Metre: ṭawīl, rhyming in -ūʿu. The pointing is the print's own. wushāt, plural of wāshī, “talebearer, slanderer”: the watchers of love poetry, who would betray the lovers, here asleep while the poet wakes; hujūʿ, “sleepers”, plural of hājiʿ. nāhīka qalban, “sufficient for you as a heart”, that is, “what a heart!”: qalban is an accusative of specification, and marūʿ, “terrified”, from rāʿa, describes it. zāda … ṭūlahu, “(my night) has increased its length”. The print points the first word of the second line اُقُوْلُ, uqūlu, with a ḍamma where the sense is aqūlu, “I say”; the printed vowel is kept. ḍūʾ, “light”, as the print points ضُوْءَ, is an old by-form of the usual ḍawʾ. The king takes up the lover's old complaint of a night that will not end.

sentences.t: وَقَوْلُ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qawlu al-ākhari
sentences.l: And the saying of the other:
sentences.i: And the words of another poet:
sentences.n: A heading for the next poem, in the nominative with its predicate left unsaid: “and (here is) the saying of the other”, al-ākhar being another poet. The madda of الآخر is the print's own.

sentences.t:
لَمَّا رَأَيْتُ النَّجْمَ سَاهٍ طَرْفُهُ * وَالْقُطْبَ قَدْ اَلْقٰى عَلَيْهِ سُبَاتَا
وَبَنَاتَ نَعْشٍ فِي الْحِدَادِ سَوَافِرًا * اَيْقَنْتُ اَنَّ صَبَاحَهُمْ قَدْ مَاتَا
sentences.tr:
lammā raʾaytu al-najma sāhin ṭarfuhu * wa-al-quṭba qad alqā ʿalayhi subātā
wa-banāta naʿshin fī al-ḥidādi sawāfiran * ayqantu anna ṣabāḥahum qad mātā
sentences.l:
When I-saw the-star, drowsy its-eye, * and the-Pole had cast upon-it slumber,
and (the) Daughters of (the) Bier in the-mourning, unveiled, * I-was-certain that their-morning had died.
sentences.i:
When I saw the star with its eye grown drowsy, and slumber cast upon the Pole,
and the Daughters of the Bier unveiled in their mourning, I knew for certain that their morning was dead.
sentences.n: Metre: kāmil, rhyming in -ātā; in subātā the alif is the accusative ending of subātan, read in pause at the rhyme; in mātā it is the rhyme's lengthened vowel. The pointing is the print's own, including the small upright alif of اَلْقٰى (alqā). sāhin ṭarfuhu, “its glance drowsy”: sāhī, “heedless, drowsy”, with ṭarfuhu as its subject; after raʾaytu one would expect the accusative sāhiyan, which the metre does not allow; sāhin may also be read as the fronted predicate of a clause, “its glance drowsy”. qad alqā ʿalayhi subātā, “had cast slumber upon it”: the subject is not named, perhaps the Pole itself or the night; the sense is that even the Pole, the star that never moves, seems asleep. Banāt Naʿsh, “the Daughters of the Bier”, are the stars of the Great Bear: four form the bier and three, the daughters, walk behind it. ḥidād, “mourning”; sawāfir, “unveiled”, of women with faces bare, as mourners went. The print points wa-banāta with a fatḥa, where the Classical accusative of a feminine plural is banāti, and gives sawāfir, normally without tanwīn, the ending -an the metre needs; both are kept. The mourners are at their station, the stars stand still, and the poet concludes that the morning itself is dead.

sentences.t: هَذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْمَلِكِ شَهْرَمَانَ وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ فَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ اللَّيْلُ قَدَّمَ لَهُ الْخَادِمُ الْفَانُوسَ وَأَوْقَدَ لَهُ شَمْعَةً وَجَعَلَهَا فِي شَمْعَدَانٍ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri al-maliki Shahramāna wa-ammā mā kāna min amri Qamari al-Zamāni fa-innahu lammā dakhala ʿalayhi al-laylu qaddama lahu al-khādimu al-fānūsa wa-awqada lahu shamʿatan wa-jaʿalahā fī shamʿadānin
sentences.l: This (is) what was of (the) affair of the-king Shahramān. And as-for what was of (the) affair of Qamar al-Zamān, indeed-he, when entered upon-him the-night, brought-forward to-him the-servant the-lantern, and lit for-him a-candle and put-it in a-candlestick.
sentences.i: So much for King Shahramān. As for Qamar al-Zamān, when night came upon him, the servant brought him the lantern, lit a candle for him and set it in a candlestick.
sentences.n: The storyteller's formula for turning from one character to another, as in the last night. ammā, “as for”, is answered by fa-innahu, whose -hu is Qamar al-Zamān; but the sentence goes on with another subject, al-khādim, the servant set at the door of the hall, a loose joining common in this text. dakhala ʿalayhi al-laylu, “the night entered upon him”, is “night came on”. qaddama li-, “to set before”. awqada, Form IV, “to kindle, light”. shamʿadān, “candlestick”, from shamʿ, “wax, candles”, with the Persian -dān, “holder”. The lantern and candle are those brought for him in the last night.

sentences.t: وَقَدَّمَ لَهُ شَيْأً مِنَ الْمَأْكَلِ فَأَكَلَ قَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: wa-qaddama lahu shayʾan mina al-maʾkali fa-akala qalīlan
sentences.l: And brought-forward to-him a-thing of the-food, and he-ate a-little.
sentences.i: He set some food before him too, and the prince ate a little.
sentences.n: shayʾan min, “a thing of”, is “some”. The print spells it شيأ, the hamza on the alif of the accusative, an old spelling of Classical شيئًا; it is kept. maʾkal, “food, what is eaten”, from akala, “to eat”; its hamza is printed. qalīlan, “a little”, an adverbial accusative.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ يُعَاتِبُ نَفْسَهُ عَلَى الَّذِي أَسَاءَ الْأَدَبَ فِي حَقِّ أَبِيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra Qamaru al-Zamāni yuʿātibu nafsahu ʿalā alladhī asāʾa al-adaba fī ḥaqqi abīhi
sentences.l: And began Qamar al-Zamān reproaching himself over that-which he-did-ill the-manners in (the) right of his-father.
sentences.i: Then Qamar al-Zamān began to reproach himself for having behaved so disrespectfully toward his father.
sentences.n: ʿalā alladhī asāʾa al-adaba, “for that he behaved ill”: alladhī here refers back to nothing and works as a bare “that”, “for the fact that he …”, a Middle Arabic use; Classical would say ʿalā mā asāʾa or ʿalā annahu asāʾa. asāʾa al-adaba, “to do ill in manners”, is “to be disrespectful”; adab is what the king said no one had yet taught him. fī ḥaqqi, “toward”, as in the last night. ʿātaba nafsahu, “to reproach oneself”, as before.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لِنَفْسِهِ يَا نَفْسِي أَلَمْ تَعْلَمِي أَنَّ ابْنَ آدَمَ رَهِينُ لِسَانِهِ وَأَنَّ لِسَانَ الْآدَمِيِّ هُوَ الَّذِي يُوقِعُهُ فِى الْمَهَالِكِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla li-nafsihi yā nafsī a-lam taʿlamī anna ibna Ādama rahīnu lisānihi wa-anna lisāna al-ādamiyyi huwa alladhī yūqiʿuhu fī al-mahāliki
sentences.l: And he-said to-himself: O my-soul, did-you not know that (the) son of Adam (is the) pledge of his-tongue, and that (the) tongue of the-human, it (is) that-which makes-him-fall into the-perils?
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “O my soul, did you not know that a son of Adam is hostage to his tongue, and that it is a man's own tongue that casts him into ruin?”
sentences.n: nafs, “soul, self”, is feminine, so he addresses it with the feminine taʿlamī, the jussive after lam. a-lam, “did … not?”, expects the answer yes. ibn Ādam, “son of Adam”, and al-ādamī, “the Adamite”, both mean simply a human being; the madda of آدم and الآدمي is printed. rahīn, “held in pledge”: a man is in pawn to what he says. huwa alladhī, “it is that which”, puts the weight on lisān. awqaʿa fī, Form IV, “to make fall into”; mahālik, plural of mahlaka, “place of ruin, peril”. فى for في again.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ ذَرَفَتْ عَيْنَاهُ بِالدُّمُوعِ وَبَكَى عَلَى مَا كَانَ صَدَرَ مِنْهُ مِنْ فُؤَادٍ مَوْجُوعٍ وَقَلْبٍ مَصْدُوعٍ
sentences.tr: thumma dharafat ʿaynāhu bi-al-dumūʿi wa-bakā ʿalā mā kāna ṣadara minhu min fuʾādin mawjūʿin wa-qalbin maṣdūʿin
sentences.l: Then shed his-two-eyes with-the-tears, and he-wept over what had issued from-him, from a-heart aching and a-heart cracked.
sentences.i: Then his eyes overflowed with tears, and he wept over what he had said, from an aching heart and a heart split in two.
sentences.n: kāna ṣadara, “had issued”: kāna with the perfect makes a pluperfect. ṣadara min, as in the last night, of words or deeds that come from someone. min fuʾādin mawjūʿin wa-qalbin maṣdūʿin, “from an aching heart and a cracked heart”, goes with bakā, naming where the weeping comes from, and rhymes, mawjūʿ / maṣdūʿ, two passive participles. fuʾād and qalb both mean “heart”; the hamza of فؤاد is printed.

sentences.t: وَنَدِمَ عَلَى مَا وَقَعَ مِنْهُ فِي حَقِّ أَبِيهِ غَايَةَ النَّدَمِ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: wa-nadima ʿalā mā waqaʿa minhu fī ḥaqqi abīhi ghāyata al-nadami wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And he-regretted over what befell from-him in (the) right of his-father (the) utmost of the-regret, and he-recited, saying:
sentences.i: He repented to the utmost of what he had done to his father, and recited:
sentences.n: nadima ʿalā, “to regret”: ʿalā marks what is regretted. waqaʿa min, “to happen from”, like jarā min in the last night, is “what he had done”. ghāyata al-nadami, “the utmost of regret”, in the accusative as an absolute object: “with the utmost regret”. This time the print sets no شعر before the verse.

sentences.t:
يَمُوتُ الْفَتَى مِنْ عَثْرَةٍ مِنْ لِسَانِهِ * وَلَيْسَ يَمُوتُ الْمَرْءُ مِنْ عَثْرَةِ الرِّجْلِ
فَعَثْرَتُهُ مِنْ فِيهِ تَرْمِي بِرَأْسِهِ * وَعَثْرَتُهُ بِالرِّجْلِ تَبْرِي عَلَى مَهْلِ
sentences.tr:
yamūtu al-fatā min ʿathratin min lisānihi * wa-laysa yamūtu al-marʾu min ʿathrati al-rijli
fa-ʿathratuhu min fīhi tarmī bi-raʾsihi * wa-ʿathratuhu bi-al-rijli tabrī ʿalā mahli
sentences.l:
Dies the-youth from a-stumble of his-tongue, * and not dies the-man from (the) stumble of the-foot;
for his-stumble from his-mouth flings-away his-head, * and his-stumble with-the-foot heals at leisure.
sentences.i:
A young man may die from a stumble of his tongue, but no man dies from a stumble of the foot:
a slip of the mouth will cost him his head, while a slip of the foot heals in its own good time.
sentences.n: Metre: ṭawīl, rhyming in -li. The pointing is the print's own. fatā, “young man”, and marʾ, “man”, both mean simply “a man”. laysa yamūtu, “does not die”: laysa with the imperfect, a plain negative. fīhi, “his mouth”, the genitive of fū, “mouth”, before a suffix. ramā bi-, “to throw, fling away”: tarmī bi-raʾsihi, “flings away his head”, that is, costs him his life; the verbs are feminine to agree with ʿathra. tabrī is hard to construe as printed: barā, yabrī, is “to pare, whittle”, while “it heals” would be tabraʾu, or with the hamza softened tabrā; the sense, and the proverb, want “heals”, and it is translated so. ʿalā mahli, “at leisure, slowly”, for ʿalā mahlin, with the kasra lengthened for the rhyme. The prince turns an old proverb on the tongue against himself.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ لَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنَ الْأَكْلِ طَلَبَ أَنْ يَغْسِلَ يَدَيْهِ فَغَسَلَ لَهُ الْمَمْلُوكُ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ الطَّعَامِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Qamara al-Zamāni lammā faragha mina al-akli ṭalaba an yaghsila yadayhi fa-ghasala lahu al-mamlūku yadayhi mina al-ṭaʿāmi
sentences.l: Then indeed Qamar al-Zamān, when he-finished from the-eating, asked that he-wash his-two-hands; so washed for-him the-mamluk his-two-hands from the-food.
sentences.i: When Qamar al-Zamān had finished eating, he asked to wash his hands, and the mamluk washed the food from his hands for him.
sentences.n: faragha min, “to be done with”: min marks what is finished. ṭalaba an yaghsila, “asked that he (might) wash”, with the subjunctive after an. ghasala lahu, “washed for him”: the servant pours the water and washes the prince's hands, as was done after a meal; min al-ṭaʿāmi, “from the food”, marks what is washed off. The one serving him is now called a mamlūk, a slave of the household, where a moment ago he was the khādim; the text does not say whether they are the same man.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ وَتَوَضَّأَ وَصَلَّى الْمَغْرِبَ وَالْعِشَاءَ وَجَلَسَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma wa-tawaḍḍaʾa wa-ṣallā al-maghriba wa-al-ʿishāʾa wa-jalasa
sentences.l: Then he-rose and made-ablution and prayed the-sunset and the-nightfall, and sat.
sentences.i: Then he rose, made his ablutions, prayed the sunset and night prayers, and sat down.
sentences.n: tawaḍḍaʾa, Form V, “to perform the ablution (wuḍūʾ)” that comes before prayer. al-maghrib, “the sunset (prayer)”, and al-ʿishāʾ, “the nightfall (prayer)”, the fourth and fifth of the five daily prayers, named by their hours with ṣalāt, “prayer”, understood. The shadda and hamza of توضّأ and the shadda of صلّى are printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning. The formula rhymes al-ṣabāḥu / al-mubāḥi.
